questions.question: To run an Agent subcommand, the syntax is `<AGENT_BINARY> <SUB_COMMAND> <OPTIONS>`. Which subcommand prints all the configurations loaded and resolved by a running Agent?
questions.explanation: `configcheck` is documented as printing all configurations loaded and resolved by a running Agent, which makes it the command for verifying which check configurations (including Autodiscovery templates) were picked up. `diagnose` runs connectivity diagnostics, and `check <CHECK_NAME>` executes one check rather than listing every loaded configuration.

questions.question: Datadog Support asks you to send the Agent's configuration files and logs for an open ticket. Which subcommand packages them into an archive and uploads it?
questions.explanation: `flare` collects the Agent's configuration files and logs into an archive (removing sensitive values) and sends it to Datadog Support, optionally tied to a case ID. `diagnose` runs connectivity checks, `health` prints the Agent's current health, and `stream-logs` shows the logs being processed by log collection in real time.

questions.question: A host sits behind a strict firewall and you suspect the Agent cannot reach Datadog. Which subcommand is documented as executing connectivity diagnosis on the system?
questions.explanation: The `diagnose` subcommand executes connectivity diagnosis on your system. `health` reports whether the Agent's internal components are healthy, `hostname` prints the hostname the Agent reports, and `configcheck` lists loaded check configurations; none of them tests network connectivity to Datadog.

questions.question: You configured a new integration and restarted the Agent, but no data appears in Datadog. What is the documented first step to see whether the integration is running?
choices: Run the `status` subcommand and look under Running Checks
Run the `health` subcommand and look under Healthy checks
Run the `version` subcommand and look under Integrations
Run the `hostname` subcommand and look under Providers
questions.explanation: The troubleshooting guide says to run the `status` command and look for the integration under the Running Checks heading; a working check is listed there without warnings or errors, and problems show up in the Config errors or Loading errors sections. `health` only reports component health, `version` prints build information, and `hostname` prints the reported hostname.

questions.question: On a Linux host, which command runs a single Agent check, as the Agent user, and prints the collected metrics to the terminal?
questions.explanation: `datadog-agent check <CHECK_NAME>` runs the specified check and prints its metrics, events and service checks; running it with `sudo -u dd-agent --` uses the same user and permissions as the Agent service. `configcheck` only prints loaded configurations, `status` shows the overall status page, and `run` starts the whole Agent rather than one check.

questions.question: A check reports rate metrics, but `datadog-agent check <CHECK_NAME>` shows no values for them. Which flag runs the check twice, one second apart, so rates can be computed?
questions.explanation: The docs recommend adding `--check-rate` to include rate metrics; it runs the check twice with a one-second pause because a rate needs two samples. `--delay` only changes how long the command waits before grabbing metrics from a run, `--json` changes the output format, and `--include-rates` is not an Agent flag.

questions.question: On a Windows host, which command, run from an elevated PowerShell prompt, prints the Agent status page including running checks?
questions.explanation: On Windows the main executable is `agent.exe` in `%ProgramFiles%\Datadog\Datadog Agent\bin\`, and its `status` subcommand prints the status page. `health` exists but only reports component health, `%ProgramData%\Datadog` holds configuration and logs rather than the binary, and `Get-Service` only shows whether the DatadogAgent service is running.

questions.question: An Agent running in Kubernetes needs DEBUG logging for a short investigation, and you do not want to recreate the pod. Which command changes the log level at runtime (Agent 7.19+)?
choices: `kubectl exec <POD_NAME> agent config set log_level debug`
`kubectl exec <POD_NAME> agent configcheck set log_level debug`
questions.explanation: Since Agent 6.19/7.19, `config set <SETTING> <VALUE>` changes runtime-editable settings such as `log_level` without a restart, which is especially useful in containers where editing `datadog.yaml` means recreating the container. `configcheck` only prints check configurations, and there is no `config reload` or `set-config` subcommand.

questions.question: You raised the Agent's verbosity with `datadog-agent config set log_level debug`. What happens to this change?
choices: It applies immediately but is lost when the Agent restarts
It is written to datadog.yaml and persists across restarts
It is queued and applied only after the next Agent restart
It is pushed to every Agent that uses the same API key
questions.explanation: Runtime changes made with `config set` take effect right away without a restart, but the documentation notes they do not persist and are lost as soon as the Agent restarts. The command does not edit `datadog.yaml`, so a permanent change still means editing the file and restarting, and it only affects the Agent you run it against.

questions.question: Which command lists the Agent settings that can be changed at runtime without a restart?
questions.explanation: `config list-runtime` lists the configuration parameters that can be changed at runtime; you can then read one with `config get <SETTING>` or change it with `config set`. `show-runtime` is not a `config` subcommand, and neither `configcheck` nor `diagnose` has a `--runtime` flag.

questions.question: A Redis container is running, but the Docker Agent never schedules the Redis check from its Autodiscovery template. Which command shows every template, including unresolved ones?
questions.explanation: The Autodiscovery troubleshooting guide uses `agent configcheck -v`; the `-v` option shows all templates, including unresolved ones, along with resolve warnings such as "No service found with this AD identifier". `status --verbose` and `diagnose --verbose` add detail to the status page and connectivity diagnostics, and `check redisdb` tries to run the check once without listing unresolved templates.

questions.question: Datadog Support opened case 1234567 and asks for a flare from a Debian host. Which command sends a flare attached to that case?
questions.explanation: The documented form is `datadog-agent flare <CASE_ID>`, with the case ID as a positional argument; you then enter the email associated with the case and confirm the upload. There is no `--case` flag or `support` subcommand, and `status` does not send flares. Without a case ID, the flare opens a new support case for your email address.

questions.question: A security team worries that a flare will leak credentials. What does the Agent do with passwords, API keys, proxy credentials and SNMP community strings when it builds a flare?
choices: Removes them from the archive before it is uploaded
Encrypts them in the archive with the org's API key
Includes them so Support can reproduce the setup
Refuses to build the flare until they are deleted
questions.explanation: A flare gathers the Agent's configuration files and logs but removes sensitive information such as passwords, API keys, proxy credentials and SNMP community strings. The command also asks for confirmation before uploading, so the archive can be reviewed first. The values are not encrypted or sent as-is, and you do not need to delete them yourself.

questions.question: The Agent has no connectivity to Datadog, so `datadog-agent flare` cannot upload the archive. What does the documentation recommend?
choices: Retrieve the archive from the local `/tmp` directory and give it to Support
Run `flare --local` so the archive uploads through a backup intake endpoint
Enable debug mode so the flare is queued and retried once the network is back
Run `diagnose` with `--send` so the logs are uploaded over the DogStatsD port
questions.explanation: The flare process first writes the archive to the local `/tmp` directory, so when connectivity is the problem you can collect that file manually and provide it to Support. `--local` only makes the CLI, rather than the Agent process, build the flare; debug mode does not queue flares; and `diagnose` has no `--send` option.

questions.question: Which Agent subcommand is documented as Windows only?
questions.explanation: `start-service`, `stopservice` and `restart-service` control the Agent through the Windows Service Control Manager and are marked Windows only in the subcommand table. `launch-gui`, `stream-logs` and `configcheck` are not limited to Windows (the GUI, for example, is enabled by default on both Windows and macOS).

questions.question: You need version 3.6.0 of the vSphere integration on a Linux host before the next Agent release ships it. Which command installs it?
questions.explanation: The syntax is `datadog-agent integration install <INTEGRATION_PACKAGE_NAME>==<VERSION>`, where the package name is the integration name prefixed with `datadog-`, run as the `dd-agent` user on Linux. `upgrade` and `add` are not `integration` subcommands, and `vsphere` without the `datadog-` prefix is not a valid package name. Restart the Agent afterwards to use the new version.

questions.question: Which `datadog-agent integration` subcommand lists every Python package installed in the Agent's environment, including Datadog integrations and their dependencies?
questions.explanation: `integration freeze` lists all Python packages in the Agent's Python environment: the `datadog-` integration packages plus the dependencies they need. `integration show <PACKAGE>` prints information such as the version of one installed integration, while `list` and `inventory` are not subcommands (the supported ones are install, remove, show and freeze).

questions.question: After running `datadog-agent integration remove datadog-vsphere`, what is left on the host?
choices: The vSphere Python package, disabled until restart
Nothing; the package and its configs are deleted
A backup copy of the package in `checks.d`
questions.explanation: Removing an integration uninstalls its Python package but does not remove the corresponding configuration folder in the `conf.d` directory, so your `conf.yaml` stays in place. The package is removed rather than disabled, and nothing is copied into `checks.d`, which is reserved for custom check code.

questions.question: A JMX-based integration collects fewer metrics than your configuration matches. Which command lists attributes that match your instance configuration but are not collected because they would exceed the metric limit?
questions.explanation: `jmx list limited` shows attributes that match one of your instance configurations but are not collected because collecting them would exceed the number of metrics allowed. `not-matching` lists attributes that match none of your configuration, `collected` lists what is actually collected, and `everything` lists every attribute with a type JMXFetch supports.

questions.question: On macOS, which command restarts the Datadog Agent service?
questions.explanation: On macOS the `launchctl` service manager controls the Agent lifecycle, and `kickstart -k` kills the running instance before starting it again, which restarts it. `kickstart` without `-k` starts the service, `kill SIGTERM` stops it, and `print` shows the service status.

questions.question: What does the `stream-logs` subcommand display?
choices: Logs being processed by a running Agent's log collection
New lines as they are written to the Agent's own `agent.log`
Metrics and events received by the DogStatsD server
Debug output from each check as it runs
questions.explanation: `stream-logs` streams the logs being processed by a running Agent, so it only shows data when log collection is enabled and configured; output can be filtered by name, type, source or service. It does not tail the Agent's own `agent.log` (read that in the Agent log directory), show DogStatsD traffic, or print check debug output.

questions.question: The Agent runs in a Docker container named `dd-agent`. Which command displays its status page, including running checks?
questions.explanation: Inside the container the Agent binary is `agent`, so `docker exec -it <CONTAINER_NAME> agent status` prints the full status page with running checks, forwarder and endpoint information. `docker ps` and `docker inspect` only report the container's state, and `docker logs` shows the container's console output rather than the status page.

questions.question: To configure the Agent to log only critical, error and warn messages, how should the local `datadog.yaml` file be modified?
questions.explanation: Each log level includes every more severe level: `WARN` logs critical, error and warn messages, `ERROR` drops warnings, and `CRITICAL` keeps only critical messages. The line must also be uncommented (remove the `#`), and the Agent restarted for the change to apply.

questions.question: What log level does the Datadog Agent use by default?
questions.explanation: The Agent logs at `INFO` by default, which the shipped `datadog.yaml` shows as the commented-out `log_level` line. `DEBUG` is meant for short troubleshooting windows because it greatly increases log volume, while `WARN` and `ERROR` are quieter levels you would opt into explicitly.

questions.question: Where does the Agent write its own log files on a Linux host?
questions.explanation: On Linux the Agent log directory is `/var/log/datadog/`, which holds files such as `agent.log`, `trace-agent.log` and `process-agent.log`. `/opt/datadog-agent/logs` is the macOS location for Agent 7.28+/6.28+, `/etc/datadog-agent/` holds configuration rather than logs, and `/var/lib/datadog/logs/` is not an Agent path.

questions.question: On a Windows host, where is the main Agent log file?
questions.explanation: Windows Agent logs live in `C:\ProgramData\Datadog\logs\`, with the main log at `agent.log`; note that `ProgramData` is a hidden folder. `C:\Program Files\Datadog\Datadog Agent\` contains the binaries (such as `bin\agent.exe`), `conf.d` holds integration configuration, and `C:\Windows\Temp\Datadog` is not an Agent path (the MSI installer writes its own log to `%TEMP%`).

questions.question: A Mac runs Agent 7.50. In which directory should you look for `agent.log`?
questions.explanation: Starting with Agent 7.28 and 6.28, macOS Agent logs are written to `/opt/datadog-agent/logs`. Older macOS Agents used `/var/log/datadog`, which is still the Linux location. `/opt/datadog-agent/etc/` holds configuration such as `datadog.yaml`, and `/Library/Logs/Datadog` is not an Agent log path.

questions.question: Traces from an instrumented application are not reaching Datadog, although host metrics are. Which Agent log file is the most relevant to inspect first?
questions.explanation: APM traces are received and forwarded by the trace-agent, which writes to its own `trace-agent.log` in the Agent log directory. `process-agent.log` belongs to live process and container collection, `jmxfetch.log` to JMX-based integrations, and `system-probe.log` to the separate system-probe component.

questions.question: With default settings, how does the Agent rotate `agent.log`?
choices: At 10 MB, keeping one backup named `agent.log.1`
Daily, keeping seven compressed backup files
At 100 MB, keeping five numbered backup files
It never rotates; OS logrotate must handle it
questions.explanation: The Agent rolls its log over every 10 MB by default and keeps a single backup (`agent.log.1`), overwriting any previous backup. Size and backup count are controlled by `log_file_max_size` (default 10485760 bytes) and `log_file_max_rolls` (default 1); rotation is built in rather than delegated to logrotate.

questions.question: You need to keep more Agent log history on disk. Which pair of `datadog.yaml` settings controls the log file size and the number of backups kept?
questions.explanation: `log_file_max_size` sets the maximum size of one Agent log file and `log_file_max_rolls` sets how many old files to keep (0 means no limit). The `logs_config` section configures log collection from your applications, not the Agent's own logs, and the other key names do not exist in `datadog.yaml`.

questions.question: What is the documented procedure to enable full debug mode for an Agent installed on a host?
choices: Set `log_level: DEBUG` in `datadog.yaml`, restart, and wait a few minutes
Set `log_level: DEBUG` in `datadog.yaml`; it applies on the next check run
Set `logs_enabled: debug` in `datadog.yaml`, then restart the Agent service
Run `datadog-agent flare --debug` to switch the Agent into debug logging
questions.explanation: Debug mode is enabled by replacing `# log_level: INFO` with an uncommented `log_level: DEBUG`, restarting the Agent, and waiting a few minutes for logs to accumulate. Edits to `datadog.yaml` are not picked up without a restart, `logs_enabled` turns on log collection rather than Agent verbosity, and `flare` has no `--debug` flag.

questions.question: You are starting a containerized Agent and want it to log at debug level from startup. Which environment variable do you set?
questions.explanation: `DD_LOG_LEVEL` is the environment variable equivalent of `log_level`, so `DD_LOG_LEVEL=debug` enables debug mode for the container Agent. `DD_LOGS_ENABLED` turns on log collection and expects a boolean, and `DD_DEBUG` and `DD_AGENT_LOG` are not Agent settings. With Helm, the equivalent is `logLevel: DEBUG` in the values file.

questions.question: You want to silence Agent logging entirely by setting the level to `OFF` in `datadog.yaml`. What is required?
choices: Also set `log_to_console: false` for it to apply
questions.explanation: The docs state that quotes are mandatory when setting the level to `'OFF'` so the value is not parsed improperly (YAML can read an unquoted off as a boolean); quotes are optional for other levels. `NONE` is not a valid level, and `log_to_console` separately controls logging to stdout.

questions.question: In a Kubernetes Agent pod with a dedicated trace-agent container, `agent config set log_level debug` worked for the agent container. How do you get debug logs from the trace-agent container?
choices: Run the same `config set` command inside it
questions.explanation: The docs state that the trace-agent container's log level cannot be changed at runtime the way the agent container's can; you must set `DD_LOG_LEVEL=debug` and redeploy. A local flare only collects existing logs without changing verbosity, and no `conf.d/apm.yaml` file controls the trace-agent's log level.

questions.question: After troubleshooting on a Linux host, the Agent logs `Permission denied` errors for files in `/var/log/datadog/`. Which command fixes the problem before you restart the Agent?
questions.explanation: The Agent's log files and the directory containing them must be owned by the Agent user `dd-agent`, so the documented fix is `sudo chown -R dd-agent:dd-agent /var/log/datadog/` followed by an Agent restart. Giving ownership to root blocks the Agent from writing, `chmod` does not change who owns the files, and changing `/etc/datadog-agent/` does not touch the log directory.

questions.question: A team set `log_level: DEBUG` in `datadog.yaml` and restarted the Agent, expecting their application's log files to appear in Log Explorer. Nothing arrives. What is the most likely reason?
choices: It sets Agent verbosity only; collecting logs needs `logs_enabled: true`
Application log files are forwarded only when `log_level` is set to `TRACE`
Debug-level output is uploaded to Log Explorer only after a flare is sent
Log Explorer requires a full host reboot after any `log_level` change
questions.explanation: `log_level` controls how verbose the Agent's own log files are. Collecting logs from applications is a separate feature that is disabled by default and must be turned on with `logs_enabled: true`, plus a log configuration for each source. No log level forwards application logs, flares go to Support rather than Log Explorer, and no host reboot is needed.

questions.question: On a systemd-based Linux host the Agent fails to start and `systemctl status datadog-agent` gives no detail. Which command displays all logs for the Agent service?
questions.explanation: For systemd systems the docs recommend `sudo journalctl -u datadog-agent.service` to display all logs for the Agent service (add `-r` for reverse order). `systemctl` has no `show-logs` action, `stream-logs` needs a running Agent and shows collected logs rather than service startup output, and `journalctl` has no `--agent` option.

questions.question: When making configuration changes in `datadog.yaml`, which statement is true?
choices: The Agent must be restarted to apply changes made to `datadog.yaml`
The Agent must be stopped before editing `datadog.yaml`, or runtime errors occur
Changes made to `datadog.yaml` are applied dynamically by the running Agent
questions.explanation: The Agent reads `datadog.yaml` when it starts, which is why the troubleshooting checklist asks whether you restarted the Agent after editing a YAML configuration file. Editing the file while the Agent runs is safe; nothing changes until the restart. Only some settings can be changed live, and that is done with `datadog-agent config set`, not by editing the file.

questions.question: After changes are made to `datadog.yaml` while the Agent is running, when does the Agent apply them?
questions.explanation: Settings in `datadog.yaml` are loaded when the Agent process starts, so edits take effect the next time the Agent starts, typically after a restart. The Agent does not re-read the file on each check cycle, and there is no `reload` subcommand; the documented procedure is to restart the Agent.

questions.question: For a Datadog Agent running on a host, what is the definitive way to determine its default configuration values?
choices: Read the Agent documentation on docs.datadoghq.com
questions.explanation: The configuration file shipped with the Agent (also installed as the fully commented `datadog.yaml.example`) lists every available option with its default value for that exact Agent version. The public docs may describe a different version, and `configcheck` prints the loaded integration check configurations rather than the Agent's default settings.

questions.question: Where is the Agent's main configuration file on a Linux host?
questions.explanation: Linux (and AIX) Agents read `/etc/datadog-agent/datadog.yaml`. `/opt/datadog-agent/etc/datadog.yaml` is the macOS location, current Agents use a YAML file named `datadog.yaml` rather than a `.conf` file, and `/var/lib/datadog-agent/` is not a configuration path.

questions.question: On Windows, where is the Agent's main configuration file?
questions.explanation: The Windows Agent reads `%ProgramData%\Datadog\datadog.yaml` (usually `C:\ProgramData\Datadog\datadog.yaml`, inside a hidden folder). `%ProgramFiles%\Datadog\Datadog Agent\` contains the binaries, `conf.d` holds integration configuration rather than the main file, and the Agent does not use a per-user `%AppData%` path.

questions.question: To enable the Redis check on a Linux host, what do you do with `/etc/datadog-agent/conf.d/redisdb.d/conf.yaml.example`?
choices: Rename it to `conf.yaml`, edit it, then restart the Agent
Edit it in place, since the Agent loads `.example` files as well
Copy its contents into `datadog.yaml` under a `redisdb:` key
questions.explanation: Each check directory ships a `conf.yaml.example`; renaming (or copying) it to `conf.yaml` and filling in your settings enables the check, followed by an Agent restart. The Agent does not load `.example` files, `checks.d` holds custom Python check code, and integration settings belong in the check's `conf.d/<CHECK_NAME>.d/` folder rather than in `datadog.yaml`.

questions.question: What is the role of a file such as `conf.d/cpu.d/conf.yaml.default`?
choices: It enables a core check out of the box unless another config exists
It holds defaults merged into every `conf.yaml` written for that check
It is a template that must be renamed to `conf.yaml` before the check runs
It stores the Autodiscovery template used for containerized services
questions.explanation: Files with the `.default` suffix are loaded automatically and define the core set of always-on checks (CPU, memory, uptime and so on); they are ignored if any other configuration is found for that check. To disable a default check, remove the file; to customize it, start from `conf.yaml.example`. Autodiscovery templates live in `auto_conf.yaml`.

questions.question: In `/etc/datadog-agent/conf.d/redisdb.d/`, which file holds the Autodiscovery template for the Redis check?
questions.explanation: Autodiscovery template files are stored in the check's configuration folder as `auto_conf.yaml`, which lets the Agent configure the check automatically for matching containers. `conf.yaml.default` enables core checks out of the box, `conf.yaml.example` is a sample to copy, and `metrics.yaml` lists the default beans collected by JMX-based checks.

questions.question: You split the `http_check` configuration into `backend.yaml` and `frontend.yaml` inside `/etc/datadog-agent/conf.d/http_check.d/`. How does the Agent treat them?
choices: It loads both valid YAML files as configuration for the check
It reads only a file named `conf.yaml` and ignores the others
It loads the first file alphabetically and skips the other one
It refuses to start the check until the files are merged
questions.explanation: The Agent loads all valid YAML files in `conf.d/<CHECK_NAME>.d/`, so complex configurations can be broken into several files; the docs use this exact `http_check` example. The file does not have to be named `conf.yaml`. The first-alphabetical rule applies only when several files point to the same log source for log collection.

questions.question: Two YAML files in an integration's `conf.d` folder both configure log collection for the same log file. What does the Agent do?
choices: Uses the first file alphabetically to prevent duplicate logs
Tails the file twice and lets Datadog deduplicate the log events
Merges both configurations and applies the union of their tags
Uses whichever of the two files was modified most recently
questions.explanation: To prevent duplicate logs, the Agent does not accept multiple YAML files that point to the same log source; it considers the files in alphabetical order and uses the first one. It does not send duplicates for backend deduplication, merge the configurations, or pick the most recently modified file.

questions.question: While troubleshooting, you want to stop a check from running without deleting its configuration. What does the documentation suggest?
choices: Rename `conf.yaml` so it no longer ends in `.yaml` or `.yml`
Add a `# disabled` comment as the first line of `conf.yaml`
Set `log_level: OFF` at the top of the check's `conf.yaml`
questions.explanation: The docs suggest renaming `conf.d/<CHECK_NAME>.d/conf.yaml` to something without a `.yaml` or `.yml` extension, such as `conf.yaml.disable`, which keeps the file but stops the Agent from loading it. A comment has no effect, `log_level` is an Agent-wide setting in `datadog.yaml` rather than a check option, and `min_collection_interval` changes how often a check runs rather than disabling it.

questions.question: A containerized Agent has `DD_SITE` set as an environment variable and a mounted `datadog.yaml` that sets a different `site`. Which value does the Agent use?
choices: The environment variable, which takes precedence
The `datadog.yaml` value, which overrides env vars
Whichever of the two values was set most recently
Neither; the Agent exits because the values conflict
questions.explanation: When a property is defined both in `datadog.yaml` and as an environment variable, the environment variable takes precedence. The file does not override it, the Agent does not compare modification times, and the conflict does not prevent the Agent from starting.

questions.question: How is a `datadog.yaml` option such as `hostname` expressed as an environment variable?
questions.explanation: Environment variable names are the option name in uppercase with the `DD_` prefix, so `hostname` becomes `DD_HOSTNAME`. The variable must match the option name exactly, so `DD_HOST_NAME` refers to a different (nonexistent) key, and a `DATADOG_` prefix or dotted names do not follow the documented convention.

questions.question: Which environment variable sets the nested `datadog.yaml` option `cmd_port: 5005` placed under `cluster_agent:`?
questions.explanation: Nested options with predefined keys are flattened by joining the keys with underscores after the `DD_` prefix, so `cluster_agent.cmd_port` becomes `DD_CLUSTER_AGENT_CMD_PORT`. Dots and hyphens are not used in these names, and `DD_CMD_PORT` sets the main Agent's own top-level `cmd_port` instead.

questions.question: An Agent on a new host is running, but no data shows up in your organization, which is on the EU site. Which `datadog.yaml` change fixes this?
questions.explanation: By default the Agent sends data to the US1 site (`datadoghq.com`); if your organization is on another site you must set the `site` parameter (or `DD_SITE`), for example `site: datadoghq.eu`, and restart the Agent. `region`, `dd_site` and `endpoint` are not the documented keys for choosing a Datadog site.

questions.question: An integration does not appear under Running Checks in the `status` output after you edited its `conf.yaml`, which may have an indentation mistake. What is the documented approach?
choices: Validate the file with a YAML parser, fix it, restart, and rerun `status`
Wait for the next check cycle, when the Agent re-reads `conf.d` automatically
Run `datadog-agent config set` to force the Agent to reload the check file
Rename the file to `conf.yaml.default` so the Agent falls back to defaults
questions.explanation: The integration troubleshooting guide says to confirm the file is in the right location with the right name, check it with a YAML parser, and restart the Agent and rerun `status` each time you change the file. The Agent does not reload `conf.d` on each check cycle, `config set` only changes runtime Agent settings, and `.default` files are reserved for core checks.

questions.question: Which pair of files correctly sets up a custom Agent check named `my_check`?
questions.explanation: Custom check code goes in the `checks.d` directory and its configuration in `conf.d`, and the names must match: `my_check.py` needs `my_check.yaml`. Swapping the directories or giving the two files different names prevents the Agent from pairing the configuration with the check code.

questions.question: You suspect the Agent is reading a different `datadog.yaml` than the one you edited. Which output shows the configuration file path the running Agent uses?
questions.explanation: The status page's Paths section lists the Config File in use along with the `conf.d` and `checks.d` directories. `configcheck` lists the check configurations the Agent resolved, `hostname` prints only the reported hostname, and `version` prints build information.

flashcards.back:
`<AGENT_BINARY> <SUB_COMMAND> <OPTIONS>`
List subcommands: `<AGENT_BINARY> --help`
Help for one: e.g. `<AGENT_BINARY> check --help`

Linux host: `datadog-agent` (use `sudo`; run checks as `sudo -u dd-agent --`)
macOS host: `datadog-agent` (e.g. `sudo datadog-agent status`)
Docker / Kubernetes container: `agent`
Windows: `%ProgramFiles%\Datadog\Datadog Agent\bin\agent.exe` from an elevated prompt

The Agent status page: version, log level, paths (Config File, conf.d, checks.d), hostnames, Collector running checks plus config/loading errors, forwarder transactions, endpoints and API key status, Logs Agent, aggregator and DogStatsD stats.
Prints all configurations loaded and resolved by a running Agent. Add `-v` to also see unresolved Autodiscovery templates and resolve warnings.

Agent 6.19+/7.19+: `config` prints the runtime config; `config list-runtime` lists editable settings; `config get <SETTING>` reads one; `config set <SETTING> <VALUE>` changes it (e.g. `log_level debug`). Changes are lost on restart.

Runs the specified check and prints its metrics, events and service checks.
Linux: `sudo -u dd-agent -- datadog-agent check <CHECK_NAME>`
`--check-rate` runs it twice (1 s apart) to include rates; `--check-times N` sets the number of runs.

Executes connectivity diagnosis on your system. Recent versions run diagnose suites that validate the Agent installation, configuration and environment (`--list` shows the suites, `--verbose` includes passed checks).

Collects the Agent's config files and logs into an archive (sensitive values removed), asks for confirmation, then uploads it to Datadog Support. With a case ID it attaches to that case; without one, your email creates a new case.

`health`: prints the current Agent health.
`hostname`: prints the hostname used by the Agent.
`version`: prints version info.
Streams the logs being processed by a running Agent's log collection (filterable by name, type, source, service). It does not show the Agent's own `agent.log`.

flashcards.front: Managing integrations from the CLI: subcommands and package names
flashcards.back:
`install <PKG>==<VERSION>`, `remove <PKG>`, `show <PKG>`, `freeze`.
Package names are prefixed with `datadog-` (e.g. `datadog-vsphere`). Run as `dd-agent` on Linux or as administrator on Windows; restart the Agent after installing.
`start-service`, `stopservice`, `restart-service`: start, stop or restart the Agent within the Windows Service Control Manager.

`sudo systemctl start|stop|restart|status datadog-agent`
Upstart systems (CentOS/RHEL 6, SUSE 11): drop `systemctl`, e.g. `sudo start datadog-agent`.
Status page: `sudo datadog-agent status`

Start: `sudo launchctl kickstart system/com.datadoghq.agent`
Stop: `sudo launchctl kill SIGTERM system/com.datadoghq.agent`
Restart: `sudo launchctl kickstart -k system/com.datadoghq.agent`
Status: `sudo launchctl print system/com.datadoghq.agent`

`jmx list matching`, `limited`, `collected`, `not-matching`, `everything`, e.g.
`sudo -u dd-agent datadog-agent jmx list collected --checks tomcat`
Starts the Datadog Agent GUI (Agent Manager) in a browser. The GUI port defaults to 5002 on Windows and macOS and is disabled on Linux (`GUI_port: -1`).

Linux: `/var/log/datadog/`
macOS (Agent 7.28+/6.28+): `/opt/datadog-agent/logs`
macOS (older): `/var/log/datadog`
Windows: `C:\ProgramData\Datadog\logs`
`agent.log`, `process-agent.log`, `trace-agent.log`, `system-probe.log`, `jmxfetch.log` (Agent 7.24+/6.24+), `dogstatsd.log` (Agent 7.46+)
`OFF`, `CRITICAL`, `ERROR`, `WARN`, `INFO` (default), `DEBUG`, `TRACE`. Each level includes all more severe ones, e.g. `WARN` = critical + error + warn. `'OFF'` must be quoted in the YAML file.

flashcards.front: Enable Agent debug mode on a host
flashcards.back:
1. Edit `datadog.yaml`
2. Replace `# log_level: INFO` with `log_level: DEBUG`
3. Restart the Agent
4. Wait a few minutes for logs
Switch back to `INFO` when done.

flashcards.front: Enable debug logging for a containerized Agent
flashcards.back: Start it with `DD_LOG_LEVEL=debug`, or at runtime (7.19+): `agent config set log_level debug`. A dedicated trace-agent container needs `DD_LOG_LEVEL=debug` and a redeploy. Helm: `logLevel: DEBUG`.
Rolls over every 10 MB and keeps one backup (`agent.log.1`, overwritten on the next rollover). Tune with `log_file_max_size` (default 10485760 bytes) and `log_file_max_rolls` (default 1).

`log_level` and `log_file` control the Agent's own logs. Collecting application logs is separate: set `logs_enabled: true` (default `false`) in `datadog.yaml` and add a log configuration for each source.

Linux: `$(pwd)/ddagent-install.log`
macOS: `/tmp/dd_agent.log`
Windows: `%TEMP%\MSI*.LOG`

flashcards.front: View Agent service logs on systemd
flashcards.back: `sudo journalctl -u datadog-agent.service` (add `-r` for reverse order). Check the service with `sudo systemctl status datadog-agent`.

flashcards.front: What goes into a flare, and where is it written first?
flashcards.back: All Agent configuration files and logs (plus tracer debug logs if APM is enabled), with passwords, API keys, proxy credentials and SNMP community strings removed. The archive is written to local `/tmp` first, so it can be sent manually if the upload fails.

Linux / AIX: `/etc/datadog-agent/datadog.yaml`
macOS: `/opt/datadog-agent/etc/datadog.yaml`
Windows: `%ProgramData%\Datadog\datadog.yaml` (hidden `C:\ProgramData` folder)

Linux: `/etc/datadog-agent/conf.d/`
macOS: `/opt/datadog-agent/etc/conf.d/`
Windows: `%ProgramData%\Datadog\conf.d`
Zero-length files in it are ignored.

`conf.yaml`: active config
`conf.yaml.example`: sample, rename to `conf.yaml` to enable
`conf.yaml.default`: core check enabled by default, ignored if another config exists
`auto_conf.yaml`: Autodiscovery template
`metrics.yaml`: default beans for JMX checks

A fully commented reference listing every option and its default, installed next to `datadog.yaml` (e.g. `/etc/datadog-agent/datadog.yaml.example`). The source is under `pkg/config/example/` in the datadog-agent repo; the old `config_template.yaml` now points there.
Only after the Agent is restarted; the file is not reloaded live. A few settings (such as `log_level`) can be changed at runtime with `datadog-agent config set`, but those changes are not saved.

Uppercase with `DD_` prefix (`hostname` -> `DD_HOSTNAME`); nested predefined keys joined with `_`; lists space-separated. Env vars take precedence over `datadog.yaml`. On systemd hosts (7.45+), put them in `/etc/datadog-agent/environment`.
`api_key` (required), `site` (default `datadoghq.com`), `hostname` (overrides auto-detection), `tags` (host tags), `env`, `log_level` (default `info`), `logs_enabled` (default `false`), `proxy`
Set a YAML list under `tags:` (e.g. `- team:infra`), or use `DD_TAGS` with space-separated values. The tags are attached to every metric, event, log, trace and service check the Agent emits.
Holds custom Python check code (default `/etc/datadog-agent/checks.d`). The matching config goes in `conf.d` with the same name: `checks.d/my_check.py` + `conf.d/my_check.yaml`.

flashcards.front: Integration missing from Running Checks: checklist
flashcards.back: Confirm the config file location and name, validate the YAML with a parser, restart the Agent, rerun `status`, then check the Agent logs for errors.

flashcards.front: Multiple YAML files for one check
flashcards.back: All valid YAML files in `conf.d/<CHECK_NAME>.d/` are loaded, so configs can be split. Exception: if several files point to the same log source, only the first file alphabetically is used.

flashcards.front: Disable a check temporarily / disable a default check
flashcards.back: Rename `conf.yaml` so it no longer has a `.yaml`/`.yml` extension (e.g. `conf.yaml.disable`). To disable a core default check, remove its `conf.yaml.default` file.

flashcards.front: What `integration install` does to config files
flashcards.back: Copies the integration's `conf.yaml.example`, `conf.yaml.default` and `auto_conf.yaml` into `conf.d`, overwriting existing ones. `integration remove` leaves the `conf.d` folder in place.
